messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Ministry Worker
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 40

A 56-year-old woman from an Oceania island nation, she works as a social ministry coordinator for a local church network. She has been married for thirty-two years. She presents for therapy after her primary care physician noticed she had not slept through the night in over a year.

She was twenty-four years old, a newlywed, and a junior social worker in a government office. She stayed late one evening to finish a case file for a family in crisis. A senior colleague, a man she trusted as a mentor, offered to walk her to the bus stop. Instead, he steered her into a storage room. She remembers the smell of old paper and dust. She remembers his hand over her mouth. She did not scream. She did not tell anyone. She told herself it was not a rape, because he did not hit her, and because she did not say no loudly enough. She went home to her husband and said nothing. She showered for forty-five minutes and told him she had a stomach bug.

For the next thirty-two years, she built a life. She raised two children. She became the person her community calls when a family loses their housing, when a teenager is in crisis, when a victim of domestic violence needs a safe place. She is good at her job. She sits with people in their worst moments and she is calm, steady, and present. She does not tell them that she knows exactly what it feels like to be trapped in a room with a person who has power over you. She does not tell them that when a client touches her arm in gratitude, her stomach turns to ice.

Three years ago, a new policy required all social workers to undergo a background check and a trauma-informed care training. The training included a module on sexual harassment in the workplace. The facilitator showed a diagram of a storage room. The room was identical to the one from thirty-two years ago. She excused herself to the bathroom and vomited. She did not return to the training. She told her supervisor she had food poisoning.

Since then, she has stopped working late. She avoids being alone in any room with a man, even her pastor. She has stopped hugging her male colleagues. She no longer visits clients in their homes if she knows the husband will be present. She makes excuses. She tells her husband she is tired. She is always tired.

She has not slept through the night in fourteen months. She wakes at 3:17 AM, every night, with the smell of dust and paper in her nostrils. Her heart pounds. She lies still, afraid to move, listening for footsteps. She does not wake her husband. She lies there until dawn, when the light makes the room safe again.

She has stopped attending church. She cannot sit in the pew without scanning the exits. She cannot take communion without feeling the hand over her mouth. Her pastor has called three times. She has not called back.

She cries in the car on the way to work. She cries in the shower. She does not cry in front of anyone. She has told no one about the storage room. Not her husband. Not her children. Not her doctor. She came to therapy because her doctor said her blood pressure was dangerously high and she was afraid of dying. She is not yet afraid of living.

She sits in the chair across from me with her hands folded in her lap. She is polite. She is composed. She apologizes for taking up my time. She says there are people who have real problems. She is one of them. She does not know this yet.
